name: Beta-propeller protein-associated neurodegeneration
aliases: static encephalopathy of childhood with neurodegeneration in adulthood

reference.source: Movement-disorder and neurogenetics textbooks with peer-reviewed reviews
clinicalPearls: X-linked dominant NBIA subtype caused by variants in WDR45, usually arising de novo and affecting mainly females (many affected males have severe or lethal presentations)

Characteristic biphasic course: global developmental delay, intellectual disability, epilepsy, and often features overlapping Rett-like behaviour in childhood, followed by a distinct second phase of progressive dystonia-parkinsonism and cognitive decline in adolescence or adulthood
Previously termed SENDA (static encephalopathy of childhood with neurodegeneration in adulthood), reflecting the apparently stable early phase before later deterioration
Sleep disturbance, stereotypies, and behavioural features are common in the early phase
MRI in the neurodegenerative phase shows iron in the globus pallidus and substantia nigra, with a characteristic T1 hyperintense halo or band around a hypointense substantia nigra
Iron-sensitive sequences (susceptibility-weighted or gradient-echo imaging) confirm the pallidal and nigral iron accumulation
WDR45 encodes a protein involved in autophagy (WIPI4), linking the disease to defective autophagic pathways
Diagnosis is confirmed by WDR45 molecular testing; treatment is symptomatic, targeting seizures, movement disorder, and behaviour
reference.pathophysiology: Beta-propeller protein-associated neurodegeneration is caused by variants in WDR45, an X-linked gene encoding WIPI4, a beta-propeller scaffolding protein essential for autophagosome formation during macroautophagy. Defective autophagy is thought to impair clearance of damaged organelles and proteins, driving progressive neuronal dysfunction. As the disease advances, iron accumulates in the globus pallidus and substantia nigra, situating it within the neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation spectrum. The gene's location on the X chromosome, combined with somatic mosaicism and presumed male lethality, accounts for the predominance of affected females.
additionalDifferentials: Rett syndrome and other MECP2-related disorders
Angelman syndrome and other neurodevelopmental epilepsy syndromes
Young-onset Parkinson disease and genetic dystonia-parkinsonism (for the second phase)
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI with iron-sensitive sequences to show pallidal and nigral iron and the characteristic substantia nigra T1 halo
WDR45 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
EEG to characterise the epilepsy in the early phase
Serum caeruloplasmin, copper, and ferritin to distinguish other NBIA subtypes and Wilson disease
redFlags: Status epilepticus or worsening seizure control
Rapid onset of parkinsonism or dystonia marking transition to the neurodegenerative phase
Acute behavioural or psychiatric deterioration with safety risk
New bulbar dysfunction with aspiration risk
reference.prognosis: The early phase is characterised by developmental delay and epilepsy that may appear relatively static for years, but a later neurodegenerative phase brings progressive dystonia-parkinsonism and dementia, usually with substantial disability. Overall the condition shortens life expectancy, though the pace of the second phase varies.
pitfalls: Labelling the early phase as a non-progressive static encephalopathy and not anticipating later neurodegeneration
Diagnosing Rett syndrome on clinical grounds without genetic testing that would reveal WDR45
Failing to obtain iron-sensitive MRI, missing the diagnostic substantia nigra and pallidal changes
Assuming the disorder affects only females and dismissing it in a severely affected male
management: No disease-modifying treatment is available; care is supportive, beginning with antiepileptic drugs tailored to the early-phase epilepsy
Symptomatic management of the second-phase dystonia-parkinsonism, including a levodopa trial and botulinum toxin for focal dystonia
Behavioural, sleep and developmental support during the early phase, addressing stereotypies and Rett-like features
Coordinated neurorehabilitation with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy, plus feeding and mobility support
Surveillance with iron-sensitive brain MRI and neurological follow-up to monitor pallidal and nigral iron and clinical deterioration
Genetic counselling for the de novo, X-linked WDR45 basis, with consideration of mosaicism testing where relevant
Multidisciplinary and palliative input as disability accrues in the neurodegenerative phase
